take_homes: Default to one agent. Split only for different access, dialect or stance, and a framework like Rumelt's kernel is what makes the synthesizer commit instead of averaging.
Most failures happen at the handoffs between agents (a number dropped, jargon smoothed over), so check where the pieces meet and diagnose sources, processing and boundary before rewriting prompts.
The crux file and the synthesis memory persist in files, so I can rerun them on the pricing question with fresh data.

monday.move: Rerun the crux and three-stance synthesis on the usage-pricing pilot with fresh data. Have the agent flag where my Q2 review and the churn article disagree, then send the briefing to the pricing working group.
monday.who: Me first, then my pricing working group
monday.stop_condition: If the briefing hides a conflict between sources, or I can't verify its main claim, I don't send it.
monday.blocker: The module is built for one person. My fourteen people have no shared place for the crux and memory files, and everyone would keep their own copy.

misconception.why: The pushing and the Rumelt kernel changed the answer more than wording did, and seams and sources caused more trouble than prompts. I still think prompts matter, so I only partly let go of the idea that better prompts are the skill.

one_line: Good hands-on hour for one person and it found something in my sources, but the lecture repeats 'start with one agent' four times and nothing shows how a team of fourteen shares it.
